title: 11 Best Social Media Design Agencies in 2026
summary: The 11 best social media design agencies, separating design-led studios from marketing-led shops, with real monthly costs and the FTC disclosure rule for paid social.
body_markdown:
**Key takeaways:**


- Social media design and social media marketing are different purchases. One makes the creative, the other buys the media and runs the account, and most agencies sell both without saying which they are actually good at.
- Volume is the whole problem. A brand running four channels needs dozens of assets a month in different aspect ratios, and the agency model that produces one beautiful campaign is rarely the one that sustains that.
- Federal wage data counts 10,375 establishments in advertising support services at an average annual wage of $53,762, less than half what full advertising agencies pay, which is where a lot of cheap social creative is actually produced.
- Paid social creative that mimics organic posting has to be recognizable as advertising before someone clicks. Federal Trade Commission guidance calls the alternative a deceptive door opener.


Ask five agencies for social media design and you will get five different products. One will send a media plan. One will send an influencer roster. One will send community management pricing. Only two will send you actual creative work.


That is not because anyone is being evasive. The category genuinely contains both the people who make the assets and the people who distribute them, and the vocabulary has never separated them.


This roundup is about the making. Every firm below was checked on its own site rather than pulled from a directory, and one well-reviewed candidate was cut when its homepage turned out to sell ecommerce email and paid ads out of Medina, Ohio. Companies past the startup stage tend to arrive at this decision with several suppliers already in play, which is the situation our[mid-market page](https://www.awesomic.com/mid-market) is written for.


## Social media design is not social media marketing


The distinction sounds pedantic until you are three months into a contract wondering why nobody has designed anything. A design-led shop is measured on the work: the carousel that stops the scroll, the template system your team can extend, the ad variant that beat the control. A marketing-led shop is measured on reach, spend efficiency and follower growth, and it will happily commission creative from a junior designer or a stock library to get there.


Plenty of good agencies do both. The question to ask is which half they would defend in a portfolio review.


Design-led social agency Marketing-led social agency


Sells you Assets, systems, templates Strategy, media, community


Judged on Craft and consistency Reach, spend, growth


Typical team lead Art director or designer Strategist or account lead


Where it struggles Media buying and analytics Volume and visual consistency


Best signal to look for A named designer on the team page A published reporting cadence


Read that table as a diagnostic rather than a scorecard. The Nix Company, for instance, states plainly that its passion is social media and its obsession is design, and it lists a digital content designer among named staff, which is exactly the signal worth hunting for. If your gap is creative output, hire the left column. If your gap is distribution, hire the right one, and expect to supply the design.


The same split runs through the wider market, and our survey of[digital design agencies](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/digital-design-agencies) maps where each model tends to sit.


## The disclosure rule that governs paid social creative


Any agency making paid social creative is working inside a set of federal rules that a surprising number of roundups never mention, and the exposure sits with the advertiser rather than the agency.


Guidance from the[Federal Trade Commission](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/native-advertising-guide-businesses) on native advertising sets the principle: it is deceptive to mislead people about the commercial nature of content. Ads that look like editorial, like a friend's post, or like anything other than advertising are judged on the net impression they leave, not on what a disclosure buried at the bottom technically says.


The operational rule is about sequence. Advertisers are responsible for making native ads identifiable as advertising **before** people arrive at the main advertising content, which the guidance calls avoiding a deceptive door opener. A label that only appears once someone has clicked through has already failed.


What counts as adequate is refreshingly practical. The guidance accepts text labels, company logos and visual cues such as background shading, outlines and borders, and for multimedia it accepts graphics, video or audio disclosures. All of those are design decisions, which is precisely why this belongs in a brief and not in a legal review three days before launch.


Short-form video carries the same duty in a harder format, and the studios that specialize in it are a separate shortlist, covered in our roundup of[video agencies for startups](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/video-agencies-for-tech-startups) .


## The 11 best social media design agencies


The firms below were selected for genuine creative capability rather than directory ranking, and each location is the one the company publishes about itself. We appear first, with our limitations stated in our own entry.


### 1. Awesomic


**Owns:** the steady output of social assets, and the brand system they have to stay inside.


Social design fails on cadence more often than on craft. The launch set looks great, then the product changes, a campaign lands, three formats get added, and by month four the feed is a patchwork of whoever was free.


Awesomic is a subscription rather than a project shop. Tasks go into the app, a vetted designer is matched the same day, and there is no cap on revision rounds. Because social sits on the same plan as brand, web and illustration, the templates, the ads and the landing page they point at stay visually consistent without a coordination meeting.


Terpli shows what that looks like over time. The AI-powered cannabis recommendation platform has worked with us for more than two years, and the social work has been continuous rather than campaign-shaped: dozens of visuals for Instagram and LinkedIn announcing new features, highlighting collaborations and showing real customer cases, running alongside flyers, email templates and improvements to the app's own onboarding screens.


That is the model in one client. Not a spectacular quarter, but a feed that still looks like the same brand two years later.


**Services:** social post and carousel design, paid social ad creative and variants, template and brand kit systems, motion and short-form video, illustration, plus web and brand design on the same plan.


**Pricing:** most social programs land on one of two published tiers. Design alone is Graphic Pack at $1,490 monthly; add no-code build, copywriting and QA and it becomes All-in-One at $2,995. Signing for a quarter brings them down to $1,190 and $2,396 respectively. The fourth option, a full-time specialist backed by a project manager, is quoted case by case.


**Proof:** Y Combinator backing, a client base beyond 4,000 companies, a project count that has passed 20,000, twin 4.9 ratings across Google Play and Trustpilot, and a hiring filter that lets through 0.82 percent of those who apply.


**Honest limits:** we design social, we do not run it. Media buying, community management, influencer contracting and paid reporting are not ours, so if you need an agency to own the spend and the calendar as well as the artwork, pair us with one of the firms below or hire from the right-hand column of that earlier table. Our[graphic design service](https://www.awesomic.com/graphic) sets out what does sit inside the plan.


[Book demo](https://www.awesomic.com/demo)


### 2. Blue Bear Creative


**Owns:** social creative built to be shared rather than served.


Working from Market Street in Denver, Blue Bear leads with a single question on its homepage, asking whether your social earns media, which is a sharper filter than most agencies apply to their own work. It displays three verified awards directly beneath it: a Shorty Awards Gold Honor, a Davey Awards Gold win and a Drum Awards Social Media win.


The site gives TikTok its own top-level navigation item rather than folding it into a services list, which tells you where the studio thinks the interesting problems are.


**Services:** social content creation, TikTok and short-form video, campaign creative, paid social assets, strategy.


**Where it fits:** brands that want work with a chance of traveling beyond the audience they paid to reach.


### 3. Socialfly


**Owns:** full-service social with the deepest awards shelf here.


Socialfly runs from West 29th Street in New York and publishes the most decorated record in this list: a Shorty Award bronze honoree and campaign winner, a five-time Vega Award winner, two appearances on the Inc. 5000, an Inc. Female Founders 100 listing and a place on Adweek's fastest-growing agencies ranking.


This is a genuinely full-service shop rather than a design studio, so creative arrives attached to strategy, influencer work and paid media. That is an advantage when you want one owner and a drawback when you only want the artwork.


**Services:** social strategy, content creation and design, influencer marketing, paid social, community management.


**Where it fits:** consumer brands that want strategy, creative and distribution bought as one thing.


### 4. The Nix Company


**Owns:** design-forward social for brands that need a look, not just a calendar.


Based on Gaston Avenue in Dallas, The Nix Company describes itself as a full-service social media and brand marketing agency, and then says something most competitors do not: its passion is social media and its obsession is design. Its team page backs that up by naming a digital content designer alongside the social managers and marketing coordinators.


Founder Jordan Nix leads as CMO, and the practice pairs audience analysis with brand strategy rather than treating social as a separate discipline from identity.


**Services:** social media management and design, brand strategy, content production, campaign creative.


**Where it fits:** mid-sized brands whose social presence looks nothing like their brand guidelines.


### 5. RXM Creative


**Owns:** luxury and beauty creative at a genuinely high craft level.


Operating from Wythe Avenue in Brooklyn since 2013, RXM was founded by creative directors Raul Mandru and Mihai Botarel, and the name is simply Raul multiplied by Mihai. Its published work runs to Loro Piana, Ray-Ban, Amika and Tata Harper, which is a client list that sets the visual standard for the rest of this category.


Its 2025 Red Dot winner profile confirms the award and also notes a strong presence in Europe alongside the New York base, so treat it as transatlantic rather than purely American.


**Services:** brand strategy and identity, social and campaign creative, immersive experiences, art direction.


**Where it fits:** premium and beauty brands where the feed has to look like the product costs what it costs.


### 6. Faceplant Creative


**Owns:** paid social creative produced at testing volume.


Planted in Austin, Texas, as its own site puts it, Faceplant is a boutique shop with an unusually clear split between paid and organic. On the paid side it lists ad creative strategy, user-generated content production, video editing and post, campaign assets, creative performance optimization and monthly content deliverables as separate line items.


That last pair matters. An agency that names creative performance optimization and a monthly deliverable count is telling you it expects to produce many variants and kill most of them, which is how paid social actually works.


**Services:** paid social ad creative, UGC production, video editing, organic social content, ad buying.


**Where it fits:** performance teams that burn through creative and need a supply line, not a campaign.


### 7. Media A La Carte


**Owns:** beauty and lifestyle content with a creator's instincts.


This New York boutique states its own numbers plainly: six years in business, more than 150 clients served and over 25 million views. Its more interesting claim is that it has built a community of almost 200,000 people across Instagram and TikTok in its own right, which is a rarer credential than an awards list.


Published clients include Laura Mercier and YSE Beauty, Molly Sims' brand stocked in Sephora, with the work covering Instagram and TikTok content creation from launches through user-generated material.


**Services:** social content creation, UGC, launch content, Instagram and TikTok production.


**Where it fits:** beauty and lifestyle brands that need content that reads as native to the platform.


### 8. Social Driver


**Owns:** social and digital communications for complicated institutions.


Social Driver works from Washington DC with additional Seattle and Chicago locations, and frames its mission as transforming complexity into clarity through people-centered digital strategies. Its capability set reaches past social into web design, audience research and broader communications.


That combination points at a specific buyer. Associations, nonprofits, healthcare bodies and public sector organizations have genuinely complicated messages and approval chains, and an agency built for consumer speed usually struggles with them.


**Services:** social media strategy and design, digital advertising, website design and build, audience research, communications.


**Where it fits:** mission-driven and public sector organizations with layered approvals and dense subject matter.


### 9. We Are Social


**Owns:** globally scaled, culturally led social creative.


We Are Social describes itself as a socially-led creative agency based in New York and Los Angeles, part of a network of more than 1,200 people, and its stated specialism is understanding behavior inside online communities and subcultures rather than platform mechanics.


Its published work includes a Sony campaign built around Jeopardy's problem of an authority trapped in a demographic cul-de-sac, which is a fair sample of the altitude it operates at. This is enterprise-scale creative with the process and cost that implies.


**Services:** social strategy and creative, influencer marketing, campaign production, cultural insight and research.


**Where it fits:** large brands running coordinated social work across markets.


### 10. LYFE Marketing


**Owns:** accessible social design for small and mid-sized businesses.


Based in Atlanta, LYFE runs a dedicated social media design service rather than treating design as a byproduct of management, covering profile assets and channel-specific graphics with an emphasis on a consistent visual identity across accounts.


One caution about the sales copy rather than the service: its page quotes engagement statistics, including an average number of social accounts per person and daily minutes spent, without naming a source or a date. Use the agency, not the numbers.


**Services:** social media design and graphics, social media management, paid social, email marketing.


**Where it fits:** smaller teams that need competent, consistent design without an enterprise engagement.


### 11. Spark Social Agency


**Owns:** boutique social creative with senior attention.


Spark positions itself on a trade every small agency claims and few articulate as neatly: the creativity and agility of a small studio with the impact a large one is expected to deliver. Its own framing is connection, conversions and community, in that order.


It publishes no street address, which is worth noting alongside the pitch. Ask where the team sits and who will actually be on your account, since the appeal of a boutique is senior people doing the work rather than selling it.


**Services:** social media strategy, content creation and design, community management, paid social.


**Where it fits:** brands that want a small senior team rather than a named agency and a junior pod.


## What social media design costs


Pricing here is set almost entirely by throughput. Two agencies can quote the same monthly figure while one delivers eight assets and the other forty, so compare deliverable counts before you compare invoices.


Engagement type Monthly or project range Biggest variable


One-off campaign creative set $2,500 to $15,000 Number of concepts, formats, shoot or no shoot


Monthly organic content design $2,000 to $8,000 a month Asset count, channels, revision rounds


Paid social ad creative at test volume $3,000 to $12,000 a month Variant count, video share, iteration speed


Template and brand kit system $4,000 to $20,000 Number of templates, handoff format, training


Full-service social retainer $6,000 to $30,000 a month Whether media, community and influencer are included


Design subscription $1,490 monthly and up Asset throughput and the breadth of work included


Where that money lands is worth understanding. For 2024 the[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/2024/a/industry/541890.csv) logged 10,375 advertising support establishments with a workforce near 93,000, paid $53,762 a year on average. That is under half the average at full advertising agencies, and it describes the production layer where a great deal of low-cost social creative is actually made. Cheap output is not automatically bad output, but the gap explains why quotes in this category vary by a factor of ten. Our comparison of[creative design agencies](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/creative-design-agencies) covers how those tiers map onto delivery models.


## Building a system instead of a stream of posts


Agencies get hired to make posts and end up making the same decisions forty times. A system prevents that, and it takes about a week to specify:


1. Define the asset types you actually publish, with exact dimensions for each channel.
2. Build editable templates for the recurring formats, and name who is allowed to edit them.
3. Set a type and color specification for social that resolves the cases your brand guidelines skip, like text over photography.
4. Decide the disclosure treatment for paid and partnership content before the first ad runs.
5. Agree a monthly deliverable count and what a revision round includes.
6. Keep one shared source of truth for approved assets, with dead versions removed.


Point four is the one that reliably gets skipped, and it is cheap to design in and expensive to retrofit across a live campaign. Point two is where the compounding happens: once your team can produce routine assets from templates, the agency's hours move to the work that actually needs an art director. Getting the input right matters as much as the output, and the mechanics of[writing a creative brief](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/crafting-a-good-creative-brief-unlock-business-results-faster) decide most of it.


## Choosing between them


Start by naming the gap honestly. If your feed looks inconsistent, hire design capability: Blue Bear, RXM, The Nix Company or a subscription. If your problem is that nothing is being posted or measured, you need a full-service agency such as Socialfly or Social Driver, and the creative will come attached.


Match the sector too, because visual fluency is not transferable in this category. Beauty and luxury work sits naturally with RXM and Media A La Carte; regulated and institutional communication with Social Driver; performance-led testing with Faceplant; multi-market brand work with We Are Social. Agencies that span several disciplines at once are a different purchase again, which our look at[full-service creative agencies](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/full-service-creative-agencies) unpacks.


Then press on volume, because it is the only variable that reliably predicts satisfaction. Ask how many finished assets a month the fee covers, what happens when you need a format that was not scoped, and who does the work when the art director is on another account. The third question is the one that separates a senior boutique from a senior pitch.


## FAQs


### What is the difference between a social media design agency and a social media marketing agency?


A design agency produces the creative: posts, carousels, ad variants, templates and short-form video. A marketing agency owns strategy, media buying, publishing and community management, and often subcontracts or juniorizes the design. Many firms sell both, so ask which half they would defend in a portfolio review before you sign.


### How much does social media design cost per month?


Ongoing organic content design typically runs $2,000 to $8,000 a month, paid social creative at testing volume runs $3,000 to $12,000, and a full-service retainer including media and community starts around $6,000. Subscription pricing opens at $1,490 monthly. Compare monthly deliverable counts rather than headline fees, since the same price can mean eight assets or forty.


### Do we need separate creative for each platform?


Yes, at minimum in aspect ratio and text treatment. A single design resized across four channels reliably underperforms, because feeds crop differently, safe zones differ, and what reads on a desktop LinkedIn post disappears on a vertical phone screen. Ask any agency to quote per-channel variants explicitly rather than assuming a resize is included.


### Who is responsible if a social ad is not properly disclosed?


The advertiser carries the exposure. FTC guidance is clear that a paid post must be identifiable as advertising before someone engages with it, and burying a label after the click does not cure the problem. Specify the disclosure treatment in the creative brief so it is designed in rather than added under pressure.


### Should we hire an agency or build social design in-house?


Hire in-house when your volume is high, your subject matter is specialized and the role is genuinely full-time. Use an agency or a subscription when volume swings with campaigns, when you need several disciplines at once, or when you cannot keep a single designer challenged enough to stay. A template system reduces the cost of either path, so build one before you decide. Organizations running several creative suppliers at once should weigh the coordination cost too, which our view of[integrated creative services](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/integrated-creative-services) sets out.
